judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Buyer-default remedy is internally contradictory: Seller is 'entitled to, as liquidated damages not to exceed $50,000, either a $50,000 letter of credit or cash equivalent', and the same paragraph then says 'the parties may seek any other remedy available at law or in equity', so whether the $50,000 is an exclusive cap is unresolved. 'Award and Assignment of the Option to Purchase', 'Any subsequent Buyer', and the revocation sentence are undefined and sit oddly with the five-day cure structure.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The liquidated-damages cap collides with the final sentence and with Section 21's fee-shifting, and the letter-of-credit obligation refers to an Assignment of the Option handled in Section 24 but nowhere else made an obligation of this Agreement. Section 17's time-is-of-the-essence clause also sits against a five-day post-notice cure right.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Injury beyond the ordinary wear and tear' and 'an appropriate deduction from the purchase price' are both vague, and the repair-or-deduct election is not clearly given to either party. The stray semicolon after 'improvements' is a minor mechanical flaw.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It contradicts Section 6, under which Buyer accepts the Property 'in the condition existing on the date of closing... including all faults... whether now or hereafter existing', and the deduction remedy has to be squared with the fixed price mechanics of Section 2. Section 12 separately handles condemnation, leaving the boundary between the two.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Substantial' is defined circularly as a portion that 'would impair or otherwise affect the intended use', and 'otherwise affect' has no boundary; the first sentence is also a fragment with a period where a comma belongs, so the trigger and the consequence are grammatically severed. 'Intended use of the Real Property' uses a term not otherwise defined in the Agreement.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 1 assigns to Buyer Seller's interest in awards for street takings and changes of grade, whereas this section gives all awards to Seller if Buyer terminates. 'Real Property' appears nowhere else, where the defined term is 'Property'.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause is written in option-agreement language — 'during the period of this Option including any extension periods', 'Optionee', 'Optionor' — inside a purchase and sale agreement that has no option period and no such defined parties. 'Any other due diligence matters deemed reasonably prudent' is an open catch-all after an enumerated list.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The whole instrument defines only 'Seller' and 'Buyer' (recitals and Section 1), so Optionor/Optionee and 'the period of this Option' can only be reconciled by importing the Real Estate Option Agreement referenced in Sections 3 and 24. It also sits against Section 6, in which Buyer acknowledges it has already completed its investigation.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Buyer's notice address is left entirely blank, and the deemed-receipt sentence covers mail and courier but not the personal delivery option expressly permitted. Whether the GSA 'copy to' is a condition of effective notice is not stated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The blank Buyer address interacts with Sections 4, 10 and 12, all of which make written notice the trigger for termination rights and cure periods, so the mechanic on which those provisions depend is incomplete. Section 24 makes GSA a necessary signatory to amendments, which does not explain its notice role here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The representation reads 'no commission... is payable to any other person or entity', where 'other' has no antecedent because no broker is named — a small mechanical oddity that could be read as excluding a party's own broker. Otherwise short and definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No other provision addresses brokerage or indemnity for broker claims, so nothing contradicts it. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Such other acts... as may be reasonably necessary' is a standard further-assurances formula whose vagueness is inherent but rarely operative on its own. Little concrete to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps with Section 8(a)(iv)'s further-documentation duty, which is capped by the 'extraordinary obligations' limit that does not appear here; the overlap is mild rather than contradictory. Section 28's cooperation duty is similar in kind.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard time-is-of-the-essence wording with a clear business-day extension rule; 'every provision hereof in which time is an element' is broad but conventional. Little ambiguity in the words themselves.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is hard to apply to a document whose date is blank and whose Closing date is only 'a mutually agreeable date' within ninety days (Section 8(a)), and it cuts against the five-day cure periods in Section 10 and the open-ended Section 5 survey duty. Those tensions are real but modest.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A boilerplate headings clause with settled meaning and no vague term. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It would only matter if a heading conflicted with text; Section 26's heading ('Utilities/Utilities Relocations and Costs') is broader than Section 7(c)'s, but the clause resolves rather than creates that problem. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Pure number-and-gender boilerplate; definite and self-contained. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No other provision turns on singular/plural usage in a contested way. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The laws of the state in which the Property is located' is indirect but unambiguous given Section 1 (Detroit, Michigan); 'permitted assigns' implies an assignment consent requirement that appears nowhere. That implication is the only soft edge.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Agreement contains no assignment clause, yet Section 24 and Section 10 both contemplate assignment of the Option by GSA and 'any subsequent Buyer', so what makes an assign 'permitted' is unstated. A federal-instrumentality purchaser also raises a question about state-law construction that the clause does not address.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Prevailing party, as determined by the court' is self-defining and the recovery is limited to costs and reasonable fees. Little ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits alongside Section 10's liquidated-damages cap of $50,000, raising a question whether fees may be added to that cap, but the clauses are not squarely opposed. Otherwise consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Short and definite: amendments must be written and 'executed by each party hereto', with counterparts permitted. Nothing vague in isolation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 24's final sentence requires amendments to be 'executed by the Buyer, Seller and the Government, acting by GSA', which is a different and stricter rule than 'each party hereto' since the Government is not a party to this Agreement. That is a direct conflict between two operative provisions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Remain in effect until fulfilled, up to and including the time of completion of any improvements to be built thereon and the written acceptance of occupancy' fixes survival by reference to construction and occupancy events that this Agreement does not govern or define. Whether 'until fulfilled' and the occupancy date are alternatives or cumulative is unclear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It states a different survival horizon from Section 7's closing warranty that the representations 'will continue to be true and correct on each day hereafter', and it depends on improvements and a GSA occupancy acceptance found only in the separate Option/lease arrangements referenced in Sections 13 and 24. Reconciling the two survival formulas is a genuine problem.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause says the Agreement 'cancels and supersedes all prior agreements' and 'is entire in itself' while simultaneously preserving the Real Estate Option Agreement (whose date is left blank) as an equally operative document, so the integration is self-contradictory on its face. 'No promises... other than those expressly contained herein' then refers back only to this Agreement, not the Option.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its amendment sentence requires GSA's execution, contradicting Section 22's 'executed by each party hereto', and its preservation of the Option is what makes Sections 3 (Permitted Exceptions), 10 (Award and Assignment of the Option) and 13 (Optionor/Optionee) intelligible — or not. This is the hinge provision for whole-instrument coherence.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One short prohibition, definite in scope and with no vague term. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No provision elsewhere grants a recording right or requires a memorandum; Section 3's deed is separate. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The representation is a near-copy of Section 7(c) but adds 'Gas' and drops 'for its current use', and the cost sentence uses 'terminations, and relocations' with a stray comma and the intruded page number ('after 8 closing'). 'All public and quasi-public and private utilities' places an unbounded cost obligation on Buyer.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The two utility representations (this and Section 7(c)) differ in scope for no stated reason, and the allocation of all relocation costs to Buyer is in tension with the representation that utilities are available 'without any special charge, assessment or apparatus' and with Section 9's proration of 'expenses and charges in connection with ownership and use'. That duplication-with-variation is the clearest inconsistency here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard counterparts language; 'any one of which shall be considered an original' is settled. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 22 already contains a counterparts sentence for amendments, so the two overlap without contradicting. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Will cooperate with the Buyer to secure all necessary government approvals' is an undefined effort standard with no deadline or cost allocation, and 'the tax incremental reimbursement shall belong to the Buyer' is stated without identifying which reimbursement or when title to it passes. 'Less any setoff' introduces a term the Agreement never defines.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates the final sentence of Section 2 but with 'less any setoff' in place of 'less any deductions', and Section 2 conditions Seller's remaining $1,000,000 on Buyer's receipt of the same TIF proceeds this section awards to Buyer. The two provisions must be read together to know who gets what and neither supplies the promised list of setoffs or deductions.
